_notes: E3 §9: foundations. Seventy scenes of petitioning, founding, running, sending out, and being outlived by a house. Gates: foundation:* flags from systems/religious/founding, charter, foundationYear; charter:<dial>:<option>; foundation:work:<id>. Effects on the house go through the `foundation` target: budget, reputation:<key>, vocation, revise:<dial>, fail, invite.

events.title: The Corridor After the Petition
events.body: The petition is on the chapter's table and the province has read it, which means the corridor has: a house, in a diocese most of them have driven through, for a work they associate with you. {@confrere} asks, at recreation, why there and why now, in the voice men use when they mean something else, and the room waits for the answer.

choices.label: Say the need is there, and name it
choices.outcome: You name the diocese's shortage and the bishop's letter and the parish nobody can staff, and the room hears a need and not a wish, which is the difference between a petition and a career, and {@confrere} nods and says he had wondered. It is what the chapter will hear too.

choices.label: Say you want to build something, and are not ashamed of it
choices.outcome: It is honest and the room likes it less: a friar who wants is a friar the chapter watches. {@confrere} says nothing, which is a kind of answer, and the petition is read that week as ambition with a good address.

choices.label: Say the provincial asked you to put it in writing
choices.outcome: It is not quite true and everyone knows roughly how true it is, and the corridor moves on, and the petition goes forward with a story attached that the provincial will hear before the chapter does.

events.title: The Provincial's Questions
events.body: {@provincial} has read the petition twice, he says, and has three questions, which he asks in the order a man asks them who has decided nothing: who goes with you, what it costs the year the money is short, and what happens to the house if you are moved in five years. He waits with the pen down.

choices.label: Name the men, and say you have spoken to them
choices.outcome: You have, quietly, and he knew, and it is either presumption or preparation depending on how the vote goes. He writes the names down. The petition is a plan now and not a hope, and a plan can be refused on its merits, which is better.

choices.label: Say the men are the province's to choose
choices.outcome: It is the correct answer and he hears the care in it, and asks the second question, and you answer that one too, and he says the chapter will want to hear you say all of it in that voice, and it does.

choices.label: Say the house would survive you because the charter would
choices.outcome: He says charters are paper and men are men, and that he has seen four foundations outlive their founders and two not, and that the two had good charters. He writes something down that is not a name.

events.title: Two Petitions
events.body: There are two petitions before the chapter this year and the other one is {@confrere}'s: a house in a diocese with a warmer bishop than yours and a plan thinner than yours, and the province can afford one. The corridor has already decided it is a race, and the two of you are expected to behave as if it is not.

choices.label: Propose to him that the two be joined into one
choices.outcome: He takes it badly for a day and well after that, and the joined petition names both of you and neither as founder, and the chapter likes a thing with two men behind it, and the province remembers that you were the one who offered.

choices.label: Let the chapter choose between them
choices.outcome: It chooses, on need, and the corridor watches the two of you at the table for a year, and whichever way it went the other man's friends remember it, and so does he.

choices.label: Withdraw yours for this year
choices.outcome: He gets his house and you get the reputation of a man who stepped aside, which is worth something in a province and nothing in a diocese, and the provincial says next year, and means it or does not.

events.title: Dinner With the Bishop
events.body: The bishop of the diocese you have petitioned for has asked you to dinner, alone, at the residence, which means he has heard and wants to look at you before he decides whether to write the letter. There is a second course and a long silence in it, and then he asks what the house would be for, in his diocese, in one sentence.

choices.label: Say it would be for his priests, who are short
choices.outcome: It is true and it is what he wants: a house that lightens his year. He says he will write, and does, and the letter is in the file before the chapter votes, which is the order things should go in.

choices.label: Say it would be for the order's work, which is his diocese's gain
choices.outcome: He hears an order that will do what it likes in his diocese, which is what orders do, and he is not wrong. He says he will consider it, which he does, slowly, and the letter is late and careful when it comes.

choices.label: Say it would be for God, and let the sentence sit
choices.outcome: He is a bishop and has heard that sentence from every religious who ever wanted something, and he smiles and says so, and then says that he happens to believe you, and writes.

events.title: After the Refusal
events.body: The chapter said no and the corridor is kind about it, which is worse. {@old_friar} stops you after Vespers and says that he petitioned twice for a house in 1979 and got it in 1983 and it is still there, and that the province refuses a thing the first time to see whether the man wants it or wants to have wanted it.

choices.label: Thank him, and ask which diocese he would try next
choices.outcome: He has opinions, all of them thirty years old and two of them still right. You take notes. The second petition, when it comes, is his as much as yours, and he votes for it from a wheelchair.

choices.label: Say you are done with it
choices.outcome: He says that is what he said in 1979, and goes to bed. You are not done with it and both of you know it, and the corridor, which watched the exchange, files it.

choices.label: Say the chapter was never going to say yes to you
choices.outcome: It is partly true and entirely the wrong thing to say to a man who was on the chapter, and he says, gently, that it was closer than you think, and that bitterness is the one thing the second vote will not forgive.

events.title: The Chancery's Letter
events.body: The province voted for your house and the bishop killed it in two paragraphs, and the letter is on the table at recreation because {@prior} left it there, and the men are reading it in the way friars read a bishop's letter, aloud, with the voices. The second paragraph regrets. The first thanks the order for its history.

choices.label: Write to the bishop yourself, once, without asking anything
choices.outcome: A page that thanks him for his consideration and names one thing the diocese lacks that a house could give, and asks for nothing. He does not answer. Two years later, when the see changes, the new bishop finds the letter in the file and asks who wrote it.

choices.label: Ask the provincial to raise it at the bishops' conference
choices.outcome: He does, or says he will, and nothing comes of it that year, and the province learns that its foundations are hostage to a diocese's temper, which it knew.

choices.label: Let it lie, and let the men have their joke
choices.outcome: The voices go on for a week and then it is old, and the letter goes in the file, and you have not said a word against a bishop in the hearing of men who would repeat it, which is a discipline the diocese notices later.

events.title: A Bishop Writes to the Province
events.body: A bishop of the territory has written to the provincial asking, in a paragraph that took him some trouble, whether the order would consider a house in his diocese: a parish nobody can staff, a university without a chaplain, a Catholic population that is younger than his priests. The provincial has sent the letter round the houses, which is how a provincial asks who wants it.

choices.label: Raise your hand, on paper
choices.outcome: You write that you would go, and why, and the provincial has a name to put beside the letter, which is what he wanted. The invitation stands in the file with yours clipped to it.

choices.label: Suggest a man better suited than you
choices.outcome: You name {@confrere}, who is, and he is asked, and goes or does not, and the provincial notes that you can see past yourself, which is rarer than the other thing.

choices.label: Say nothing; a letter round the houses is not a letter to you
choices.outcome: The letter goes round and comes back with two names on it, neither yours, and the bishop's invitation stands for a few years and then does not.

events.title: The Provincial's Silence
events.body: You said no to a foundation the provincial asked you to lead, and he has been correct with you since, which in a provincial is a temperature. {@confrere}, who was asked second and said yes, is packing. He asks, not unkindly, whether you would mind telling him why.

choices.label: Tell him the truth, whatever it was
choices.outcome: You tell him: the fear, or the work you could not leave, or the bishop you could not stomach. He listens and says he understands, and goes, and the house he founds is a good one, and it is his.

choices.label: Say you were not the man for it, and that he is
choices.outcome: It is generous and half true, and he takes the half, and writes from the new house at Christmas, every year, which is a kindness and a reminder.

choices.label: Say you regret it already
choices.outcome: He says the provincial would take that badly and you should not say it to him, and you do not, and it sits in you for a decade as the house you did not found.

events.title: The Second Petition
events.body: It has been three years since the chapter said no and {@old_friar} has been asking, every month, whether the second petition is written. It is written. It names a different diocese, a warmer bishop, a thinner plan, and the same work, and it is a better petition than the first because you know now what a chapter hears.

choices.label: File it
choices.outcome: The chapter reads a man who came back, which it likes, and a plan that learned, which it trusts, and the corridor says the friar is stubborn in the tone it uses for the ones who get things built.

choices.label: Wait one more year for the province's finances
choices.outcome: The treasurer says the year after is better and it is, and the petition goes in with money behind it, and the wait was the plan's and not the fear's, which the province can tell.

choices.label: Leave it in the drawer
choices.outcome: It stays there. {@old_friar} stops asking, which is the saddest thing he has done, and the house you did not found is a place you drive through, once, years later, and think nothing you say aloud.

events.title: The Treasurer's Questions
events.body: The province's treasurer, who has never petitioned for anything and has stopped four foundations by asking the right question at the right chapter, has sent you two pages of questions about the house you want: the roof, the insurance, the year the diocese's stipends do not come, the men's cars, the retirement burden the province carries already. He wants answers in numbers.

choices.label: Answer every question, in numbers
choices.outcome: You spend a fortnight on it and the answers are honest, which means some of them are bad, and he reads them and says at chapter that the plan knows what it costs, which from him is a benediction.

choices.label: Answer that foundations are acts of faith and the money follows
choices.outcome: He says he has heard that from four men and three houses are closed, and reads the sentence aloud at chapter in his flat voice, and the room laughs, and the petition is a little lighter for it.

choices.label: Ask the provincial to answer the treasurer for you
choices.outcome: The provincial does, in a paragraph, and the treasurer notes that the founder could not, and the chapter notes that the provincial had to, and both are true and neither helps.

events.title: The Young Founder
events.body: You are young for this and everyone has said so: the corridor, the council, the treasurer in the margin of his questions. {@provincial} says it directly: a man of your years founding a house is rare, watched, and enormously exposed, and he wants to know whether you know that, and whether you want it anyway.

choices.label: Say you know it, and want it anyway
choices.outcome: He nods as if a box were ticked and says that the province will be harder on you than on an older man and that this is not unfair, and that if it works you will have thirty years in a house you made, which no older founder gets.

choices.label: Ask whether an older man should lead it and you go as his vicar
choices.outcome: He says it is the humble answer and possibly the right one, and thinks about it, and the petition is amended to name an older man and you under him, and the chapter passes it easily, and it is his house.

choices.label: Say you will wait ten years
choices.outcome: He says ten years is a long time to want a thing and that most men who say it do not petition again, and that he hopes you are not most men. You are or you are not, and the decade decides.

events.title: The First Night
events.body: The men are asleep and the house is not yet a house: boxes in the hall, a chapel with a table for an altar, the bishop's decree framed and not yet hung, the charter in your desk in your own hand. You are its prior because you wrote it, and the province is a long way off, and the diocese does not yet know your name.

choices.label: Sit in the chapel until Lauds
choices.outcome: You do, and the house begins in the way you meant it to, with a man in the chapel before anyone was required to be, and the men who wake early find you there, and it becomes the thing they say about the house's first year.

choices.label: Sit at the desk and write the horarium
choices.outcome: By Lauds there is a bell schedule and a rota and a list of what the kitchen lacks, and the house begins as a thing organized, which it needed, and the men wake to a prior who has already decided the day.

choices.label: Sleep; the house will be there in the morning
choices.outcome: It is, and so are you, rested, which the year will need, and the first day begins with a prior who is not already tired, which the men notice more than a vigil.

events.title: The Men You Were Sent
events.body: The province sent you men and one of them is {@confrere}, who did not ask to come and has said so at every meal: a good friar, a hard man, sent because his prior could spare him, which is the province's way of saying the opposite. He is at the door of your office with a list of what the house is doing wrong.

choices.label: Take the list, and do three things on it
choices.outcome: Two of the three were right and the third was his, and he sees that you took it seriously, and stays, and is the house's best man by the third year and its prior by the tenth, and never once says he asked to come.

choices.label: Ask the provincial to take him back
choices.outcome: The provincial does, and sends no one in his place, and the house is a man short and a grievance lighter, and the man tells the province for years that the founder could not bear to be told.

choices.label: Give him the one job he cannot complain about: the money
choices.outcome: He takes the books and the books are perfect and the complaining stops because he is now the man the complaints go to, and it is either wisdom or cowardice and it works.

events.title: The Bell at Five
events.body: The charter says strict and the bell says five, and {@confrere} has not been at Lauds three mornings running and is not sick. In a province house it would be a word at recreation. In a house that exists to keep the bell, it is the charter's first test, and the men are watching to see whether the charter is a document or a rule.

choices.label: Speak to him, in the office, as the rule
choices.outcome: He comes to Lauds the next morning and every morning after, and does not forgive you for a year, and the men know the bell is a bell, and the serious young men who come later come for exactly that.

choices.label: Ask him what is wrong
choices.outcome: Something is, and he tells you, and it is not the bell, and you deal with the thing and the bell follows, and the house learns that the rule has a man in it, which is a different house from the other one and also a good one.

choices.label: Let it go; the house is new
choices.outcome: It goes, and so does the bell, a little, and by Advent Lauds is the prior and two others, and the charter's word strict is a word, and the province, when it visits, says so.

events.title: The Neighbours Hear Vespers
events.body: The office is sung, in Latin, with the windows open because the chapel has no air, and the street has noticed. Two letters came this week: one from a neighbour who says it is the most beautiful thing on the block and one from a neighbour who says it is six o'clock every evening and she has a baby. {@prior} of the old house, visiting, says both letters are the house's reputation being born.

choices.label: Close the windows and buy a fan
choices.outcome: The baby sleeps and the office is the house's again, and the reputation grows more slowly and inside the walls, where a reputation for the office belongs.

choices.label: Invite the street to Vespers
choices.outcome: Eleven people come the first Sunday and forty by Lent, some of them from parishes across the diocese, and the house is the place where the office is sung, and the pastor of the parish down the road has an opinion.

choices.label: Move Vespers to seven
choices.outcome: The baby sleeps and the men grumble and the office is sung at seven for thirty years, and nobody remembers why, and it is the first thing a successor changes.

events.title: The Order's Rite
events.body: The conventual Mass is in the order's own rite, restored from books the studium had not opened in fifty years, and the province has come to look. {@provincial} sits in the back with his hands folded and afterward says, in the corridor, that it was beautiful and that he has had four letters about it and would like to know what to say to them.

choices.label: Say it is in the charter the chapter approved
choices.outcome: It is, and he knows it, and says so to the four letters, and the rite stays, and the house is the thing the province means when it argues about itself, which was the risk and is also the point.

choices.label: Offer to keep it for feasts and the ordinary rite for the days
choices.outcome: He says it is a reasonable compromise and the letters will accept it, and the men who came for the rite are a little quieter at recreation, and the house is a house with a beautiful feast day and an ordinary Tuesday.

choices.label: Ask him what he would say
choices.outcome: He says he would say that the order has more than one way of praying and this house has chosen the oldest, and that a province that cannot hold one such house is not a province. He says it well, and you write it down and use it for years.

events.title: The Bishop Comes to Dinner
events.body: {@bishop} has come to dinner in the first year, as he said he would, with his secretary and a bottle, and has walked the house and said the chapel is small and the kitchen is good, and now at the table he says that he has a parish nobody can staff and wonders aloud whether the house might.

choices.label: Say yes, if the province agrees
choices.outcome: It is the correct order and he knows it and likes that you know it, and the province agrees, and the house has a parish before it has a second vocation, and is tied to his shortage and his goodwill for a generation.

choices.label: Say the house is too new to spread itself
choices.outcome: He hears a prior who protects his men, which bishops respect and do not enjoy, and the parish goes to a diocesan man who is also too new, and the bishop remembers both things.

choices.label: Say in three years, when the men are formed
choices.outcome: He writes it down. In three years he asks again, and the house says yes or no from strength, and the bishop, who kept the note, respects the man who set the date and kept it.

events.title: The First One
events.body: A young man came to Vespers in Advent and stayed for supper and has now written a letter that says, in six pages, that he would like to enter, and that he would like to enter here, in this house, and not in the province, which he does not know exists. He is the house's first, and he is not, on the six pages, obviously suitable.

choices.label: Send him to the vocations director, as the province requires
choices.outcome: The director sees what you saw and also what you did not, and he enters or does not on the province's judgment and not yours, and the house's first vocation is handled the way the last one will be, which the province notices.

choices.label: Take him yourself for a year, before anything is written
choices.outcome: He lives in the house as a guest and prays the office and washes the pots, and at the end of the year he enters or goes home, and either way he was formed by you, which the men who come after will hear about.

choices.label: Tell him kindly that it is not the life for him
choices.outcome: It may not be. He goes, and marries, and brings his children to Vespers for thirty years, and one of them enters, and the house's first vocation was the second generation.

events.title: The Year the Money Is Short
events.body: The stipends did not come, or came late, and the roof did the thing roofs do in a house the province bought cheaply, and the treasurer's two pages of questions have turned out to be prophecy. {@confrere}, who keeps the books, puts them on your desk open at the page.

choices.label: Ask the province for a loan
choices.outcome: The province lends, at chapter, after a discussion the treasurer enjoys, and the house owes the province, which is a relationship, and the roof is fixed by Lent.

choices.label: Find a benefactor
choices.outcome: There is one, there is always one, a widow or a builder or a man whose son you buried, and the roof is fixed and a plaque goes up and the house owes a layman, which is a different relationship.

choices.label: Cut the house to the bone for a year
choices.outcome: No cars, no heat in the corridors, the men in coats at Matins, and the roof waits, and the house learns what it can do without, and the austerity becomes a story the vocations tell each other.

events.title: The University's President
events.body: The house is embedded in the university and the president has asked for a meeting, which means the university has an agenda and the house is on it. He is not a friar and has never been anything like one. He would like the chaplaincy to be more visible, the friars to teach two courses each, and the chapel hours to fit the academic calendar.

choices.label: Give him two of the three
choices.outcome: The courses and the visibility, and the chapel keeps its hours, and he is satisfied for a year, and the negotiation is permanent, as the charter said it would be, and the house learns to hold its ground in a room with a board.

choices.label: Hold the charter's line on all three
choices.outcome: He is polite and the faculty appointments are slower to come and the chaplaincy budget is reviewed, and the house is the order's and not the university's, and pays for it.

choices.label: Give him all three
choices.outcome: The house is the university's chaplaincy with a habit, and the students love it, and the men are teachers first and friars in the evenings, and the province says at visitation that it cannot tell whose house this is.

events.title: The Neighbourhood Decides
events.body: The house was founded for the poor and the poor have noticed: the door is knocked on at every hour, the kitchen feeds twenty a night, and {@confrere} says at recreation that the house has no cloister because the street is in it. A man slept in the chapel last night. The men are divided about whether that is the charter or the end of it.

choices.label: Keep the door open; that is the charter
choices.outcome: The chapel is where the street sleeps in winter and the office is said around it, and the house is loved in six blocks and thin everywhere else, and it is exactly what you wrote.

choices.label: Set hours, and keep them
choices.outcome: The door is open from eight to eight and the chapel is the men's at night, and the street learns the hours, and the house has a cloister and a kitchen and is both things, which takes a rule to hold.

choices.label: Build the shelter the charter implies
choices.outcome: The house buys the building next door with money it does not have, and the street sleeps there, and the friars go over at night, and the diocese sends a caseworker, and the house has a work that outlives it.

events.title: The Parish's Council
events.body: The parish the bishop entrusted to the house has a council, and the council had a pastor for nineteen years before it had friars, and it has come to the first meeting with a list: the Mass times, the music, the school, and the question of whether the friars will be here in five years or whether the order does what orders do.

choices.label: Promise them the order is here to stay
choices.outcome: You cannot promise it and you do, and the council relaxes, and the parish is the house's, and in eleven years when the province wants the men back the promise is on the record in the council's minutes.

choices.label: Say the order stays while the province can staff it, and mean it
choices.outcome: They hear a man who will not lie to them and do not like the answer, and the parish takes three years to trust the house, and does, on that footing, which is the only footing that lasts.

choices.label: Take the list, and change the Mass times first
choices.outcome: The Mass times move to what the house can keep with its office, and the council is annoyed for a season and then is not, since the friars are at every Mass, and the school question waits.

events.title: The Provincial's Visitation
events.body: {@provincial} has come for the canonical visitation and has interviewed every man alone, as the constitutions require, and now sits in your office with a notebook he does not open. He says the house is what the charter said. He says one of the men is unhappy and will not say why to him. He says the province is watching the house more closely than the house knows.

choices.label: Ask him which man
choices.outcome: He will not say, which is correct, and you go through the house in your mind and find him, and speak to him, and the unhappiness is real and fixable, and the visitation report says the prior knows his men.

choices.label: Ask what the province is watching for
choices.outcome: He says it is watching to see whether the house is yours or the order's, and that the answer so far is both, and that both is fine for ten years and not for thirty, and closes the notebook.

choices.label: Thank him, and ask nothing
choices.outcome: He is a little surprised, and writes a shorter report than he had planned, and the province reads a house with nothing to hide, which is nearly true.

events.title: The Deanery Considers the Friars
events.body: The diocese's priests have a new house of religious in their deanery and have opinions about it, which {@dean} conveys at the deanery meeting in the form of questions: whether the friars will take the Saturday confessions the pastors are tired of, whether the sung office will draw their people, and whether the house intends to be a parish by another name.

choices.label: Offer the deanery the Saturday box and nothing else
choices.outcome: The pastors send their penitents and keep their people, and the house is useful without being a rival, and the deanery decides the friars are all right, which in a deanery is a permanent verdict.

choices.label: Say the house will do what the charter says and the people will decide
choices.outcome: It is true and it is a declaration of war heard as one, and the pastors watch their Sunday counts, and one of them writes to the bishop, and the bishop, who invited the house, does nothing, and the pastor remembers.

choices.label: Ask the dean to dinner, alone
choices.outcome: He comes, and eats, and says what the pastors are really afraid of, which is being outshone, and you say the house will preach at their missions if they ask, and they ask, and the deanery is the house's friend by Easter.

events.title: The Austere Kitchen
events.body: The charter says austere and the kitchen has taken it to heart: one dish, no wine on weekdays, the heating off in the corridors, and {@confrere}, who is sixty and came from a house with a cook, has stopped eating with the community and is seen buying sandwiches in the town. The young men, who came for the austerity, have noticed.

choices.label: Make an exception for the old, quietly
choices.outcome: He eats in the infirmary, which is a room with a heater, and the young men understand that the rule bends for age and not for taste, and the house is austere and humane, which is harder than either.

choices.label: Hold the rule for everyone
choices.outcome: He asks for a transfer and gets it, and the young men respect the house and the province thinks it is cruel, and both readings survive for twenty years.

choices.label: Soften the rule for everyone
choices.outcome: Wine on Thursdays and heat in the corridors, and he comes back to the table, and the young men are a little disappointed, and the house is moderate, which the charter did not say.

events.title: The First Death in the House
events.body: {@old_friar} came to the house in its second year because he asked to and the province was glad to have him somewhere, and has died in the room off the chapel, at Lauds, with the men singing. He is the house's first dead. The house has no cemetery and no custom and the men are looking at you for both.

choices.label: Bury him here, and make the custom
choices.outcome: The bishop gives a corner of the parish cemetery and the house buries its first man with the office sung over him, and every man after is buried there, and the house has a place where it ends, which a house needs.

choices.label: Send him home to the province's cemetery
choices.outcome: The province buries him among the men he lived with for fifty years, which is right, and the house has no dead, which is a lightness and a lack.

choices.label: Ask the men what he would have wanted
choices.outcome: They know, since he told them at recreation for a year, and it is here, and they bury him, and the custom is the men's and not the prior's, which is the better kind.

events.title: The Reporter
events.body: A reporter from the diocesan paper, or the city one, has heard that a house of friars has opened in a diocese that has not seen a new religious house in forty years and would like a morning: the office, the kitchen, a photograph in the chapel, and a quotation about why now. The men are divided between vanity and dread.

choices.label: Give her the morning
choices.outcome: The piece is kind and slightly wrong and the photograph is beautiful, and the house is known in the city before it is known in the province, and three letters come from young men who read it.

choices.label: Give her the office and nothing else
choices.outcome: She sits through Lauds and writes about the singing and asks no one anything, and the piece is short and true, and the house is a rumour rather than a fact, which suits it.

choices.label: Decline
choices.outcome: She writes it anyway from the street, and it is less kind, and the house learns that the press is not a thing one declines, only a thing one shapes or does not.

events.title: The Man Who Should Not Enter
events.body: A vocation came through the house and the house formed him and he is a year from vows, and {@novice_master}, who is not yours, has written that he has doubts about the man: not sin, not scandal, a hardness, a way of using the rule on other people. The man is the house's, the first the house formed, and everyone in the province knows it.

choices.label: Back the novice master
choices.outcome: He goes home, angry, and the house lost its first, and the province notices that the founder did not protect his own against the order's judgment, and the next vocation is watched a little less.

choices.label: Defend him to the provincial
choices.outcome: He takes vows, on your word, and is the house's for forty years, and is exactly what the novice master said, and is also its best preacher, and the province says you were right and wrong and cannot decide which.

choices.label: Ask for another year before vows
choices.outcome: The province gives it, and the year is hard for him and for the house, and at the end he has softened or has not, and the vow is taken or not on what a year showed, which is what a year is for.

events.title: The Recall
events.body: The province is short everywhere and the letter is the one every founder dreads: {@provincial} needs a man for a house that is collapsing and the house he is taking him from is yours, and the man is {@confrere}, who runs the work the house was founded for. The letter is polite and is not a question.

choices.label: Send him, with a good letter
choices.outcome: He goes, and the work limps for two years, and the province sees a founder who gave up his best man without a fight, and remembers it the next time the house asks for something.

choices.label: Offer another man instead
choices.outcome: The provincial takes him, since what he needs is a body and not a name, and {@confrere} stays, and the house learns that a founder who bargains can keep what matters, and the province learns the same.

choices.label: Refuse, in writing
choices.outcome: The provincial takes him anyway, since he can, and the refusal is in the file, and the house is the one that fought the province in a shortage, which some of the province admires and the council does not.

events.title: The New Provincial's Opinion
events.body: The chapter elected a provincial from the other side of the province's fault line and he has visited, and been gracious, and has said in the corridor that the house is a fine thing and that he wonders whether it is the order's future or its museum. The men heard him. The house sits at odds with the province as written, which the charter said it might.

choices.label: Invite him to preach at the house's feast
choices.outcome: He comes, and preaches well, and sees the church full of young people, and says at chapter that the museum has visitors, which is a joke and a concession, and the house is safer for it.

choices.label: Write to him about what the house is for
choices.outcome: A page, without heat, about the charter and the vocations and the office. He answers in a paragraph that says he read it. It is filed, and it is either useless or the thing that saves the house at the next chapter.

choices.label: Say nothing, and keep the charter
choices.outcome: The house keeps the bell and the office and the rite, and the provincial reassigns one man a year to somewhere the province needs him, which is his right, and the house is smaller each Advent and more itself.

events.title: The School's Board
events.body: The school under the house has a board of parents who did not take vows and have opinions about the tuition, the uniform, the Latin, and the fact that two friars in the halls are two more than the last principal had. The chairman would like to know who runs the school: the house, or the board that raises its money.

choices.label: Say the house does, under the charter
choices.outcome: The board takes it and two members resign, and the school is the house's, and the money is harder for a year and then is not, since the parents who stayed wanted a school run by friars.

choices.label: Say the board does, and the house teaches
choices.outcome: The board runs a good school and the friars teach in it, and the school grows and the friars are staff, and the province asks at visitation why the house has a school it does not govern.

choices.label: Write a governance document, together
choices.outcome: It takes a year and a lawyer and it is the best thing the house has done for the school, and the chairman and the prior sign it, and it outlives both, which was the point.

events.title: The Students on Sunday Night
events.body: The chaplaincy has filled: the Sunday night Mass is standing room and the confessions after it go past midnight, and the students have started coming to the house's own Vespers, which the men love and the horarium does not. {@confrere} says the house is a student centre with an office attached.

choices.label: Keep both, and let the men be tired
choices.outcome: They are, for years, and the house is the place the students come and the vocations come from, and the men who wanted a cloister transfer out and the men who wanted this transfer in.

choices.label: Put a wall between the chaplaincy and the house
choices.outcome: The students have their chapel and the house has its own, and the men sleep, and the vocations that come now come to the order and not to a friar they knew, which is either healthier or fewer.

choices.label: Assign one man to it entirely
choices.outcome: He is the chaplain and nothing else, and burns brightly for five years, and the house has a work with a name on it, and when he moves the students ask where he went.

events.title: The Shelter's Neighbours
events.body: The shelter is full and the block has a petition: needles in the alley, a man asleep in a doorway, a parent who will not walk her children past. The councilman has called. The parish council has an opinion. The men who work the shelter say the block has always had needles and only noticed when the friars gave the men a bed.

choices.label: Hold a meeting on the block, and stand in it
choices.outcome: It is two hours of anger and at the end a woman says her brother slept there last winter, and the block does not sign, and the councilman finds something else, and the shelter has neighbours who know its name.

choices.label: Tighten the shelter's rules
choices.outcome: Curfew, a search at the door, a list, and the shelter is smaller and calmer and the block is quiet, and the men who cannot keep the rules sleep in the alley, which was the point of the shelter.

choices.label: Close it for the winter
choices.outcome: The block is grateful and the men who worked it are not, and it does not reopen, and the house is a house that had a shelter, which the poor of the city remember longer than the block does.

events.title: The Journal's Enemy
events.body: The house's journal has printed a piece by one of the men that a cardinal did not like, and the cardinal's office has written to the provincial, and the provincial has forwarded the letter without comment, which is a comment. The man who wrote it is at your door, holding the letter, and is not sorry.

choices.label: Stand by the piece, and say so to the provincial
choices.outcome: The provincial answers the cardinal's office that the journal is a journal and the house stands by its men, and the house is known in Rome, which is a mixed blessing that lasts, and the man writes better after.

choices.label: Print a note in the next issue
choices.outcome: A paragraph that regrets any offence and withdraws nothing, which is the form, and the cardinal's office is satisfied with the form, and the man is not, and writes elsewhere.

choices.label: Pull the piece from the website and apologize
choices.outcome: It is done, and the journal is safe, and it is read less after that, since a journal that pulls is a journal that will pull, and the man asks for a transfer to a house with a press that stands.

events.title: The First Class of Novices
events.body: The house is a house of formation now and the first class is four young men in the novitiate wing, and you are forming the men who will fill the house and vote in chapters for forty years, and you know it every time you walk past their door. {@novice_master}, whom the province assigned, has his own ideas about how, and one of them is not yours.

choices.label: Let the novice master form them his way
choices.outcome: They come out his, which is mostly yours, since he was chosen against the charter, and the house has a formation that is the order's and not one man's, and the men trust it because it is.

choices.label: Take the conferences yourself
choices.outcome: Two a week, on the charter and the office and the work, and the four come out yours in a way the province can see across a room, and it is the deepest thing you will do and the most dangerous.

choices.label: Split the year between you
choices.outcome: Half the conferences his and half yours, and the four hear two readings of one charter and choose between them, which is what formation is for, and one of them is prior here in thirty years.

events.title: The Weekend That Went Wrong
events.body: The retreat wing is full every weekend and this one is a parish group from across the diocese whose pastor did not come, and something is wrong in the group: a marriage ending in the corridor, a man drinking in his room, the retreat director, who is {@confrere}, asking you at midnight what a retreat house does when the retreat is the problem.

choices.label: Stay up with him, and see it through
choices.outcome: You do, both of you, until Sunday, and the marriage does not end that weekend and the man is driven home by a friar, and the group tells its pastor the friars were there, which is the reputation the retreat house wanted.

choices.label: Send the group home early
choices.outcome: They go, and the pastor is embarrassed and the house is not, and the wing is quieter for a month and the diocese's groups book elsewhere for a year.

choices.label: Tell him it is his weekend and go to bed
choices.outcome: He handles it, and it is his, and he is the retreat director from then on in the way that matters, and does not need you at midnight again, which is either delegation or abdication and worked.

events.title: The Hospital's Nights
events.body: The hospital chaplaincy has the house on call and the call comes at two: a death, a birth going wrong, a family in the corridor. {@confrere} has taken it for a year and has stopped sleeping, and the hospital's director of pastoral care would like a second friar on the rota, and the house has no second friar to give.

choices.label: Take the second rota yourself
choices.outcome: The prior at the hospital at two in the morning, for a year, and the house sees it and the hospital sees it, and the reputation the city keeps longest is the house's now, and you are tired for a year.

choices.label: Put every priest of the house on the rota
choices.outcome: Everyone takes a night, and the office is thinner on the mornings after, and the house is a hospital house and knows it, and the young men who came for the choir have to decide.

choices.label: Give the hospital back half the rota
choices.outcome: The hospital finds a deacon, and the house keeps its nights, and the reputation is smaller and the men are rested, and the director of pastoral care is polite about it.

events.title: The Bloc Across the Diocese
events.body: The sung office has done what the charter said it would: there is a bloc now, people from across the diocese who drive to the house on Sunday and would drive to the moon, and they have opinions about the house's Mass and the diocese's, and a newsletter, and a pastor in the next deanery who has written to the bishop about them by name.

choices.label: Say they are the house's people and the house will stand with them
choices.outcome: The bishop reads the pastor's letter and yours and does nothing, and the bloc grows, and the house is known as the bloc's house, which is a reputation with a shape the diocese can see from anywhere.

choices.label: Send half of them back to their parishes, in a homily
choices.outcome: You preach it: that a parish is a parish and the house is a house, and some go, and some stay and are quieter, and the pastor withdraws his letter, and the bloc becomes a congregation, which is smaller and lasts.

choices.label: Stop the newsletter
choices.outcome: It stops, and starts again from someone's kitchen, and the house has no control of it now, and the bishop asks whether the friars edit it, and you say no, which is true and does not sound it.

events.title: The Benefactor's Condition
events.body: A man has offered the house more money than it has seen, for the chapel, on a condition: his name over the door, a Mass a month for his family in perpetuity, and a word with the prior about the house's politics, which he has read about and has views on. He is not a bad man. He is a man with money and views.

choices.label: Take it, with the name and the Mass and not the word
choices.outcome: The chapel is built and his name is over the door and the Mass is said monthly for a century, and the word is not had, and he is disappointed and gives anyway, since the chapel was the thing.

choices.label: Decline the condition, and so the money
choices.outcome: He goes, and gives it to the cathedral, and the chapel waits ten years, and the house is a house that did not sell its politics, which the men tell the vocations, who came for that.

choices.label: Have the word, and take the money
choices.outcome: An hour in the parlour in which he says what he thinks and you say what the charter says and neither changes, and the chapel is built, and he comes to Vespers and does not mention it again.

events.title: The Old Friar Who Wants to Come
events.body: {@old_friar} has written from a house the province is thinning, asking to spend his last years here, in the house he watched you found, in a room off the chapel if there is one. He is eighty and will need care the house is not built for and will give the house a thing it does not have, which is a man who remembers 1970.

choices.label: Say yes, and find the room
choices.outcome: He comes, and is carried to Lauds by the novices, and tells them what the order was and was not, and dies in the house in four years, and the young men who carried him are different friars for it.

choices.label: Say the house cannot care for him
choices.outcome: It cannot, and the province's infirmary can, and he goes there and writes once, and the house is a house of young men, which is the charter and also a lack.

choices.label: Say yes, and hire a nurse
choices.outcome: The nurse is the house's first lay employee and the old friar its first patient, and the house learns what a community does with its old, which the province's houses learned fifty years ago.

events.title: The Men Ask for a Change
events.body: The house chapter has met without you, which it may, and has a request: a change to one line of the charter, put by {@confrere} in a voice that has been practised. They are not wrong that the house has changed. They are not right that the charter should. The men are waiting, and the founder is in the room, and everyone knows whose paper it is.

choices.label: Hear them out, and change the line
choices.outcome: You change it, at the chapter, in front of them, and the charter is the house's now and not yours, which is the thing that lets it outlive you, and it costs you a line you loved.

choices.label: Hold the line, and say why
choices.outcome: You say why, for twenty minutes, and the room is not persuaded and does not push, since the founder held, and the line stands until the founder is gone, when it is the first line changed.

choices.label: Ask them to live the line for one more year and vote again
choices.outcome: They do, and the year answers the question, and the vote is the house's on evidence and not on the founder's feeling, and it goes one way or the other and stands.

events.title: Choosing the Heir
events.body: The house is large enough to send men out and the province has said so, and the question is who leads it, and it is the deepest question the house has asked you: one of the men you formed, and the daughter house will be his reading of the charter and not yours. There are two, and they are not the same man, and {@confrere} has an opinion about which.

choices.label: The stricter one, who will keep the office
choices.outcome: He goes, and the daughter house sings the office and keeps the bell and in thirty years is stricter than the mother, and the province has two houses on one side of its line, which the province notices.

choices.label: The looser one, who will hold the men
choices.outcome: He goes, and the daughter house is kinder than the mother and its office is shorter, and the men there love him, and it is a different house, which is what a daughter is, and you feel it every time you visit.

choices.label: Ask the house chapter to choose
choices.outcome: They choose, and it is the man you would not have, and he goes, and the daughter house is theirs and not yours in two ways at once, and you have taught the house to choose its own heirs, which the province calls a constitution.

events.title: A Letter From the Daughter House
events.body: The daughter house has written, in the heir's hand, its first year's account: the men, the money, the office, and one paragraph that says the charter's line on the liturgy has been read, on reflection, a little differently, and that the house hopes the founder understands. It is a good letter. It is not your house.

choices.label: Write back, and bless the difference
choices.outcome: You do, in a page that says the charter was always a reading and his is a reading, and the daughter house keeps the letter framed, and its men read it as permission, which it was.

choices.label: Go and see
choices.outcome: You go, and sit in the daughter's chapel through its office, which is not yours, and say nothing, and the heir walks you to the car and says thank you for not saying anything, and you drive home and are quiet for a week.

choices.label: Write back, and say what the charter meant
choices.outcome: A page about the line and what it meant and why, and he answers that he understood it and read it anyway, and the two houses are two houses after that, and both know it.

events.title: The Heir's Own Foundation
events.body: The heir has written from the daughter house to say that it is large enough now to send out a house of its own, and that he has chosen his man, and that he wanted the founder to know before the province did. The man he has chosen is one you never met. It is the third generation, and you are a grandfather in a way the vow did not foresee.

choices.label: Go to the sending, and say nothing at the table
choices.outcome: You go, and sit at the far end, and the third house goes out from the second with a charter that is two readings from yours, and you recognize about half of it, and the half you recognize is the office.

choices.label: Write to the man you never met
choices.outcome: A letter to a stranger about a paper he has read and you wrote, and he answers, carefully, and the letters go on for a decade, and he is the one who writes the house's history, later.

choices.label: Let it be theirs
choices.outcome: It is theirs, and it goes out, and you read about it in the provincial's newsletter, and it is the first thing of your line you had no hand in, which is the whole point and also a grief.

events.title: The Two Houses Disagree
events.body: The mother house and the daughter have disagreed in public, at chapter, about a thing the province asked both of them: whether the line should take a work the diocese offered. The heir voted one way and the house you founded the other, and the province, which had hoped the line would vote as one, has watched it split, and is not sorry.

choices.label: Take the mother house's side, in the room
choices.outcome: You do, and the line loses the vote and keeps its argument, and the heir does not speak to you for a year, and does after, and the province has learned that the line is not a bloc, which the province wanted to know.

choices.label: Take the heir's side, against your own house
choices.outcome: The house you founded is astonished, and the heir is not, since he knew you would, and the vote goes his way, and the mother house learns that the founder is the line's and not the house's, which is a lesson it needed.

choices.label: Abstain, and let the two houses be two
choices.outcome: It is the only thing a founder can do at that chapter, and both houses know it, and the vote goes as it goes, and the line is a line of houses and not a party, which the province writes down.

events.title: The Vicariate
events.body: The houses of your line are a vicariate now, with a vicar and a seat, and the chapter that erected it has asked, through {@provincial}, whether the founder would be its first vicar, and whether he understands that a vicariate is the beginning of a province and that a province is a thing that argues with the one it came from.

choices.label: Take it
choices.outcome: You take it, and the vicariate is a small province with a large founder, and the mother province is polite and watchful, and in twenty years the vicariate is a province or is not, and you were its first.

choices.label: Name the heir instead
choices.outcome: He takes it, and the vicariate is his and the line is his, and you are the founder, which is a title and a photograph, and the province sees a man who built a thing and gave it away, which it had not seen.

choices.label: Say the line should have no vicar yet
choices.outcome: The chapter is puzzled and agrees, and the vicariate is a name on paper for a decade, and the houses are houses of the province, which is either humility or the thing that stops a province from being born.

events.title: The Heir Is Elected
events.body: The chapter has elected the heir provincial: the man you formed in the house you founded, over the men who formed you. He has written the night of the election, one paragraph, that says he will try to be the province's and not the line's, and that he wanted you to know before he had to be.

choices.label: Write back, and tell him to be the province's
choices.outcome: You do, and he is, and the line is treated like any other for four years, which is what it needed and what it resents, and the province sees that the founder wanted no faction, and believes it.

choices.label: Ask him for one thing for the house
choices.outcome: You do, a small thing, and he gives it, and it is the only thing you ever ask, and the province notices that too, and calls it a favour, once, at a table.

choices.label: Say nothing
choices.outcome: He waits for the letter and it does not come, and he governs as if it had, and it is the right thing and the cold one, and you are not sure for years which you meant.

events.title: Visiting the Daughter House
events.body: You are at the daughter house for a week, as a guest, in the room they keep for the founder, and the office is at the hour you set and the bell is the bell, and something is different that you cannot name until the third day, when you see that the men do not look at the prior before they speak. They look at each other.

choices.label: Say it to the heir, as praise
choices.outcome: He says he learned it from watching you, which is not true, and you both know it, and the thing he did that you did not is the reason the daughter house is the one the province points to.

choices.label: Bring it home
choices.outcome: You try, and the house you founded is too used to looking at you, and it takes years and your leaving, and the successor gets the credit, which is how it should be and is not how it feels.

choices.label: Say nothing, and be a guest
choices.outcome: You are a guest for a week and leave, and the room is kept for you, and you come every year, and it is the house of your line you love best and it is not yours, and you never say the first half aloud.

events.title: The Daughter House Closes
events.body: The daughter house is closed: the vocations did not come or the bishop changed or the province took the men, and the heir has written to say so, in a letter that blames himself for a thing that was mostly the diocese's, and asks whether he may come back to the mother house, or whether the founder would rather not see him.

choices.label: Tell him to come home
choices.outcome: He comes, and is the house's again, and says nothing about the daughter for a year and then says everything, at recreation, to the young men, who learn that foundations fail and men come home, which is the truest thing the house teaches.

choices.label: Tell him to petition for another
choices.outcome: He is astonished, and does, in three years, and the second daughter house is the one that lasts, since the man who founded it had already lost one, and the province says the line is stubborn.

choices.label: Leave it to the province where he goes
choices.outcome: The province sends him to a house that needs him and he is good there and does not write, and the line is one house shorter and one man quieter, and you did not say the thing he needed.

events.title: The Line on Paper
events.body: A novice in the mother house has drawn the line on a sheet of paper for the feast: the house, the daughters, the daughters' daughters, with the priors' names and the years, and pinned it in the corridor. It is a family tree. It has your name at the top. Several of the men have stopped in front of it and none of them has said anything.

choices.label: Leave it up
choices.outcome: It stays for the feast and then in the archive, and is redrawn every decade by a novice who adds a branch, and the last version has forty names on it and yours is small at the top.

choices.label: Take it down, kindly
choices.outcome: The novice is hurt and understands later, and the line is a line and not a dynasty, and the province, which had heard about the sheet, notes that the founder took it down himself.

choices.label: Have him take your name off it
choices.outcome: He does, and the tree begins with the house, and the men understand what you meant and the novice most of all, and it is the version that is redrawn, without a founder, for a century.

events.title: The Founder Returns to the Ranks
events.body: Your term as prior of the house you founded has run, and the chapter has elected another man, and you are a friar of the house you built, at the table, in a stall, under a prior who read your charter as a novice. He is gracious. He has already moved the bell by fifteen minutes.

choices.label: Keep your stall and your silence
choices.outcome: You do, for years, and it is the hardest thing the house asks of you and the thing the men remember longest: the founder who did not govern from the choir, and the prior who was let be a prior.

choices.label: Ask the provincial for another house
choices.outcome: He sends you, kindly, to a house that needs a man, and the house you founded has its founder's absence, which is a presence, and you come back for the feast every year and sit at the far end.

choices.label: Advise him, privately, once a week
choices.outcome: He listens, the first year, and then does not, and then asks you to stop, and the house has two priors for a year and then one, and the province hears about it from the men.

events.title: The Charter Changed
events.body: The letter from the house says it plainly: the prior has revised the charter, one line, after a chapter that voted for it, and the line is one of yours. He writes that he thought you should hear it from him. He writes that the house is well. He does not write that he is sorry, because he is not.

choices.label: Write back, and thank him for the letter
choices.outcome: You do, and say nothing about the line, and he keeps the letter, and the house is a house whose founder let it change, which is what a charter is for and what founders almost never let happen.

choices.label: Write back, and argue the line
choices.outcome: Two pages, good ones, and he answers in one, and the line stays changed, and the argument is in the archive with the charter, and the men who read both later say the founder was right and the prior was prior.

choices.label: Go, and see what the change has done
choices.outcome: You go, and it has done less than you feared and more than he said, and the house is a good house with a different line, and you sit in its chapel and cannot tell whether the thing you feel is grief or relief.

events.title: The Office Is Not Sung
events.body: You are back at the house you founded, for a feast, at seventy or near it, and the office is said. Not sung. Said, in the vernacular, quickly, by men who are kind to you and did not know the house when it sang. The prior has explained it: the men, the hours, the times. It was the single most visible thing about the house, and it is gone.

choices.label: Sing Vespers alone, from your stall
choices.outcome: You do, one evening, the old tone, and the chapel lets you, and two of the young men join in at the Magnificat, since they knew it from somewhere, and the prior says nothing, and the next feast it is sung once, for you, and after that it is not.

choices.label: Say the office with them, and mean it
choices.outcome: You say it, and it is the office, and the house is the house, and what you built was a house and not a tone, which is the thing you tell yourself in the car and half believe.

choices.label: Leave before Vespers
choices.outcome: You do, with an excuse, and the prior knows, and it is the last time you come, and the house has a founder who could not bear it, which the men tell each other with more sympathy than you would expect.

events.title: Exactly As You Left It
events.body: You are back at the house you founded, at seventy or near it, and it is exactly as you left it: the bell, the office, the rule, kept by men you never met, who know your name and use it the way the house uses a saint's, and one of them, the youngest, asks after Vespers whether it is true that you sat up in the chapel the first night.

choices.label: Say it is true
choices.outcome: He is delighted, and tells the others, and it becomes the thing they say about the house's first night, which it already was, and you are a story now, which is what a founder is for.

choices.label: Say the house is the men's and not the founder's
choices.outcome: He is a little disappointed and understands later, and tells the others that too, and the house has both stories, and the second is the one the prior tells at chapter.

choices.label: Ask him why he came
choices.outcome: He tells you, and it is the office, and the bell, and a friar he heard preach who came through this house, and you understand that the house works, and that you may go home.

events.title: The House You Founded Is Closed
events.body: The house is closed and you were its prior when it closed, and the men are in the province's other houses by Advent, and you are to be assigned by the year's consultation like anyone else. The charter is in the province archive. {@provincial} has been kind, in the way a man is kind who has to write the decree.

choices.label: Own it, at chapter, in a sentence
choices.outcome: You stand and say the house failed and that it was yours, and sit, and the chapter is silent and then goes on, and the province sees a man who does not blame the diocese or the money, and it is the thing that lets you petition again in ten years.

choices.label: Say the diocese killed it
choices.outcome: It did, partly, and the chapter hears a founder who blames, and it is filed with the decree, and the province does not think of you for a foundation again.

choices.label: Say nothing, anywhere
choices.outcome: You are assigned, and go, and do not speak of the house for a decade, and the men who were in it speak of it for you, kindly, and the silence is either dignity or a wound, and the province cannot tell.

events.title: After the Closing
events.body: A year after the house closed, you are in a house that is not yours, at a table that has its own jokes, and {@confrere}, who was one of your men, is at the same table, and has said at recreation, not unkindly, that he does not regret the years, and the table has gone quiet and is waiting to see what you say.

choices.label: Say you do not regret them either
choices.outcome: The table breathes, and the two of you are the men who were at the closed house, which is a bond the table respects, and the house you are in learns that a failed foundation is not a shame, which the province needed one house to learn.

choices.label: Say you regret the men it cost
choices.outcome: It is true and it is the wrong thing at a table, and the table is kind about it, and {@confrere} finds you after and says the men it cost do not regret it either, and you did not know that.

choices.label: Make the joke before someone else does
choices.outcome: It lands, and the table laughs, and the closed house is a thing that can be joked about, which is either healing or the thing that stops it, and you are not sure for years.

events.title: Once More
events.body: Ten years after the house closed, {@provincial} has asked, over dinner and without preamble, whether you would found another. A different diocese, a warmer bishop, a province with money this time. He says he has read the old charter. He says the second one would be better because you would know what to leave out.

choices.label: Say yes
choices.outcome: You say it before he finishes, and he laughs, and the second petition is written in a week and passes in a year, and the second house is smaller and lasts, and the men there know about the first, since you tell them.

choices.label: Say once was enough
choices.outcome: He nods, and asks someone else, and the someone else founds it well, and you are the man who founded one house that closed, which is a whole life and not a small one, and you know it by then.

choices.label: Say one of your men should, and you would go with him
choices.outcome: He likes it, and the man is asked, and says yes, and you go as his vicar, and the second house is his with you in it, and it is the better arrangement and you both know it.

events.title: The Bishop Who Invited You Is Gone
events.body: The bishop who signed the decree of erection has been moved, or retired, or died, and his successor has come to the house once, briefly, and has said at the deanery since that he inherited a great many arrangements and intends to look at all of them. The house is an arrangement. The men have heard.

choices.label: Ask to see him, and bring the charter
choices.outcome: He reads it, or looks at it, and asks what the house does for his priests, and you tell him, and he says he will see, and does, over a year, and the house is his arrangement now, which is safer than being the old bishop's.

choices.label: Wait, and keep the house's head down
choices.outcome: The house is quiet for two years and he looks at other arrangements first, and the house is the one he never got to, which is a way to survive and not a way to be known.

choices.label: Let the deanery speak for the house
choices.outcome: The pastors do, to your surprise, since the house takes their confessions and preaches their missions, and the new bishop hears from his own priests that the friars are useful, which is the only argument a bishop hears.

events.title: The Council's Proposal
events.body: The province's council has a proposal before the chapter to close the house: not for failure, since it has not failed, but for men, since the province is short, and a house that sits at odds with the province's line is a house the council can close with fewer regrets. {@provincial} has sent the proposal to you before the chapter, which is a courtesy and a warning.

choices.label: Fight it at chapter, with the numbers
choices.outcome: The vocations, the works, the money, the bishop's letter, and the chapter is moved by the numbers as it is never moved by feeling, and the proposal fails by four votes, and the council remembers the four.

choices.label: Ask the bishop to write
choices.outcome: He writes, since the house is his, and the chapter reads a bishop who wants the friars, and closing a house a bishop wants is a thing a province does not do twice, and the proposal is withdrawn.

choices.label: Accept it, and ask only that the men be sent together
choices.outcome: The chapter is astonished and the council is relieved and the men are sent together to one house, which becomes, in ten years, the house by another name, and the province did not see it coming.

effects.value: the province needed the men, and the founder let it have them

events.title: The Chapter Elects the Other Man
events.body: The house chapter has elected as prior the one man in the house who never liked the charter, and he has been correct with you since, which in a prior is a temperature. He has not changed anything yet. He has said at recreation that the house has a great deal of history for a young house, in a tone the men are still parsing.

choices.label: Support him, publicly, at the first house chapter
choices.outcome: You do, in a sentence, and the men see it, and he sees it, and it does not stop him changing things but it changes how he does it, which is slowly and with the chapter, and the house survives its second prior, which not all houses do.

choices.label: Ask for a transfer
choices.outcome: The provincial gives it, since it is the humane thing, and the house has its founder's absence and its new prior's freedom, and both use them, and the house is a different house in five years and still standing.

choices.label: Stay, and say nothing, and watch
choices.outcome: You watch, and he knows you are watching, and the house has a prior and a founder in it like two weather systems, and the men learn to read the sky, which is a skill they did not need.

events.title: The Charter in the Archive
events.body: The province archivist has written to ask whether you would like the charter of the closed house returned to you, or left in the archive with the decree of erection and the decree of closure, in the box where the province keeps the houses that did not happen. He says there are eleven boxes. He says yours is the newest.

choices.label: Leave it in the box
choices.outcome: It stays, and a novice finds it in forty years and reads it and asks his novice master who the founder was, and the novice master, who was one of your men, tells him, and the charter is read again, once, by someone.

choices.label: Take it back
choices.outcome: It is in your desk for the rest of your life and in the province's when you die, and it goes back in the box, and it is the same box, and the archivist, who is a different archivist, notes the return.

choices.label: Ask him to burn it
choices.outcome: He will not, since archivists do not, and says so, gently, and it stays in the box, and you never ask again, and the wanting to burn it was the thing that needed to happen.

events.title: The Name on the Wall
events.body: The house has put up a plaque: the year of the foundation, the bishop's name, the founder's. It is in the cloister where the men pass it four times a day. The prior did not ask you. The men think it is right. You have walked past it twice and read it both times and would like to stop doing that.

choices.label: Let it be
choices.outcome: It stays, and you stop reading it in a year, and the men never do, and it is the first thing the vocations see and the last thing the old men touch, and it is bronze and outlasts everyone in the building.

choices.label: Ask that the first men's names be added
choices.outcome: They are, all five, and the plaque is the house's founding and not its founder, and the men who were sent and did not ask to come are on the wall with you, which is where they were.

choices.label: Ask that it come down
choices.outcome: The prior refuses, kindly, and it stays, and the men tell the vocations that the founder wanted it down, which is on the plaque now in a way bronze cannot be.

events.title: The Last Man You Formed
events.body: The last man you formed in the house you founded has taken solemn vows, and you were not at the profession, since you are old or elsewhere, and he has written to say so, and to say that he read the charter in the novitiate and did not understand it and reads it now and does, and to ask one question about a line.

choices.label: Answer the question
choices.outcome: A page, on the line, and he keeps the page, and reads it to the novices when he is novice master, which he is, and the line is understood in the house for a generation because a young man asked.

choices.label: Ask him what he thinks it means
choices.outcome: He tells you, and it is not what you meant and it is better, and you write back to say so, and the line means what he said from then on, and you did not mind, which surprised you.

choices.label: Go and see him
choices.outcome: You go, old, and he is young, and you sit in the chapel you sat in the first night, and he does not know that, and you do not tell him, and it is enough.

events.title: The House Asks You Back
events.body: The house you founded has written, through its chapter, to ask whether you would let your name go forward for prior again. Its current prior is leaving; the men are divided; the founder is the one name they can agree on. {@provincial} has enclosed the letter with a note that says only that it is your decision and the chapter's.

choices.label: Let the name go forward
choices.outcome: The chapter elects you, and you are prior of the house you founded twenty years on, and it is not the same house and you are not the same man, and the second term is quieter and better and the men who remember the first are old.

choices.label: Decline, and name a man
choices.outcome: You name one of your men, and the chapter takes the name, since it came from you, and the house has a prior who was formed in it, which was always the plan, and you are the founder who did not come back.

choices.label: Go, and let the chapter see you, and then decline
choices.outcome: They see an old man and a founder and understand which one they were asking for, and choose one of themselves, and you go home, and the house has done the thing a house does when it is grown, which is choose.

events.title: The History of the House
events.body: A young friar of the house is writing its history for the anniversary and has sent you a chapter: the founding, the first men, the charter, the first years. It is well researched and slightly wrong in the way histories are, and it has a paragraph about the founder that you would not have written and cannot, on reflection, dispute.

choices.label: Correct the facts, and leave the paragraph
choices.outcome: You send three pages of corrections, dates and names, and say nothing about the paragraph, and it is printed, and it is the version of you the house has, and it is kinder than the truth and less interesting.

choices.label: Ask him to come and ask you
choices.outcome: He comes, with a recorder, for three days, and the history is longer and truer and has your voice in it, and the men read it at table for a year, and the founder is a man in it and not a plaque.

choices.label: Send it back without a mark
choices.outcome: He prints it as it is, and it is the history, and the paragraph stands, and you are what the house says you were, which is what happens to founders and is not the worst thing.

events.title: The Room Off the Chapel
events.body: You are old, and the house you founded has asked whether you would like to come home to it, to the room off the chapel where the old friar died in its fifth year, and the prior, who was a novice under you, has said that the men would carry you to Lauds, as the novices carried him.

choices.label: Go home
choices.outcome: You go, and are carried to Lauds, and the men sing, and it is the house, in the tone or not in it, with the bell or without, and you die in it, and are buried in the corner of the cemetery the bishop gave, first among the men, which was the custom you made.

choices.label: Stay in the province's infirmary
choices.outcome: It is the humble answer and the house understands it and does not, and the prior visits monthly, and the house has a founder who died elsewhere, and buries him anyway, in the corner, when the province lets it.

choices.label: Ask the daughter house instead
choices.outcome: You go to the daughter, to the room they keep for the founder, and die there, among men two readings from your charter, who sing what they sing, and it is either a joke or a blessing and the line tells it as both.

events.title: The Language of the Parish
events.body: The house's parish is half Spanish and the charter's line on the liturgy did not think of it, and {@confrere}, who has the language, says the sung Latin office is beautiful and the people who fill the Sunday Mass are not at it, and would like to know whether the house sings for the people it has or the people it wanted.

choices.label: Add a Spanish Vespers, and keep the Latin one
choices.outcome: Two Vespers, and the men are stretched, and the church is full at both, and the house is the parish's in a way the charter did not plan, and the reputation for the office is a reputation in two languages.

choices.label: Keep the Latin; the people may come to it
choices.outcome: Some do, and it is beautiful, and the parish's council says the friars sing for themselves, which is unfair and is said, and the Sunday count holds and the weekday count does not.

choices.label: Give him the parish's liturgy entirely
choices.outcome: He builds it, in Spanish, with the choir the parish had, and the house's office is the house's and the parish's Mass is the parish's, and they are two things under one roof, which is what a parish house is.

events.title: The Founder's Sabbatical
events.body: Ten years in, the provincial has offered a sabbatical: a year away, Rome or a library or a hermitage, on the ground that a founder who never leaves is a founder the house cannot learn to live without. {@confrere} would be prior for the year. The men are pretending not to have heard.

choices.label: Go for the year
choices.outcome: You go, and the house runs, and is a little different when you return and does not change back, and the year is the best thing you did for the house and the hardest thing you did for yourself.

choices.label: Take six months
choices.outcome: Six months is a long time and not a year, and the house learns half the lesson, and you learn that the house did not need you for six months, which is half the other lesson.

choices.label: Decline; the house is too young
choices.outcome: The provincial says it will always be too young, and lets it go, and offers again in five years, and you decline again, and the house never learns to live without you until it has to, which it does badly.

events.title: The Heir's Doubt
events.body: The man you have chosen to lead the daughter house has come to your office the week before he goes and said that he does not think he is the man, that he has read the charter a hundred times and does not know what he would write differently and is afraid of what he would, and asks whether a founder ever felt this.

choices.label: Say yes, the first night, in the chapel
choices.outcome: You tell him about the first night, which you have told no one, and he goes, and founds a house that is his, and tells his own heir about your first night, forty years on, in the same words.

choices.label: Say no, and that he should go anyway
choices.outcome: It is a lie in a good cause and he half believes it, and goes, and founds a house that is his, and finds out later from one of your men that you sat up all night, and forgives you.

choices.label: Say a man who doubts is the man, and that he may wait a year
choices.outcome: He waits, and the year makes him surer or does not, and he goes or another man does, and the daughter house is founded by a man who was ready, which is rarer than a man who was chosen.

events.title: The Charter Read at Chapter
events.body: The house reads its charter aloud once a year at the chapter of the feast, a custom someone started, and this year you are in the room as a guest and not the prior, and a young friar is reading it, well, in a voice that has never heard yours, and at the line you wrote at three in the morning he pauses, because it is a good line, and goes on.

choices.label: Say nothing, and let him read
choices.outcome: He reads it to the end, and the house has its charter in a voice that is not yours, which is the only way a charter lasts, and you are a guest who heard it, and it was enough.

choices.label: Thank him after, for the pause
choices.outcome: He did not know he had paused, and is pleased, and asks about the line, and you tell him, and he tells the novices, and the line has a story now, which lines need.

choices.label: Leave the room before the end
choices.outcome: You do, and the prior finds you in the cloister, and says nothing, and stands there, and it is the kindest thing a successor did for you, and you go back in for the blessing.
